DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Introducing an Off-Peak Membership
Pulse Fitness, Commercial Team, August 2026

1. Proposal
We propose introducing an off-peak membership at £29 a month from 1 October 2026, alongside our existing standard membership at £42 a month. Off-peak members would have access before 4 pm on weekdays and all day at weekends, with full access to the gym floor and to classes running in those hours.

2. Background
Pulse operates four clubs with 9,600 standard members. Membership has been flat for 18 months, while two budget gyms have opened within our catchments, both offering memberships at £22 to £25 a month. Our clubs are busy between 5 pm and 8 pm on weekdays, when the gym floor often runs at or near capacity, but quiet during weekday daytimes, when typical utilisation is around 30%.

Access-control data for May to July 2026 show that 31% of our current standard members visit exclusively in what would be the off-peak window, and a further 22% visit mostly off-peak.

3. Market evidence
A survey of 640 non-members living within two miles of our clubs, conducted in June, found that 19% would "definitely" or "probably" join at £29 a month for off-peak access. The most interested groups were retirees, shift workers, parents of school-age children and students.

Four of our six closest competitors already offer an off-peak or daytime membership, priced between £25 and £32.

4. Classes and retention
Retention is the other half of our commercial challenge. Monthly churn among members who attend at least one class a week is 2.1%, against 4.8% among members who do not attend classes. Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week to support the new membership, which should lower churn among off-peak members towards the 2.1% level. The additional classes would cost £18,700 a month across the four clubs in instructor fees.

5. Revenue projection
We expect to recruit 1,200 new off-peak members in the first year, about 300 per club, which is consistent with the survey response and the size of our catchments. At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue. After the cost of the additional classes (£224,400 a year), net additional revenue is £193,200 a year.

Because daytime utilisation is low, the additional members can be accommodated without investment in equipment or space.

6. Operational changes
Access control will be updated so that off-peak members' cards do not open the turnstiles outside their access window. Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm, giving those finishing early shifts or school pick-ups time to train. Members will be able to upgrade to standard membership at any time, and to switch between membership types with one month's notice.

7. Risks
Some standard members may perceive the off-peak price as unfair. We will communicate the change as an extension of choice. Competitor responses are possible; the budget gyms already price below our proposed off-peak rate, so we do not expect a price war.

8. Staff consultation
Club managers and front-of-house teams at all four clubs were consulted in July. Managers supported the proposal, noting that daytime classes are often under-filled and that a daytime membership would help build a regular community at quieter times. Front-of-house staff asked for clear signage and app messaging about access hours, which we will provide before launch.

9. Recommendation
The off-peak membership fills spare daytime capacity, responds to competitor offers and targets clearly identified customer groups. We project net additional revenue of around £193,000 a year and recommend launch on 1 October 2026.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm" -- Section 1 defines off-peak access as before 4 pm on weekdays; section 6 says off-peak members have weekday access until 5 pm (also into the busy 5-8 pm period the document says is near capacity). The access window contradicts itself.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week" -- The churn difference is correlational: members who choose to attend classes weekly are likely more engaged/committed to begin with (self-selection). It does not show classes cause lower churn, nor that adding classes would bring off-peak churn to 2.1%.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue." -- The projection counts only new members and ignores downgrades, although the document states 31% of the 9,600 standard members (about 2,976) already visit only off-peak and can switch with one month's notice. If they downgraded, revenue would fall by about £13 x 2,976 = £38,700 a month (about £464,000 a year), more than wiping out the projected gain.

REVIEW:
# Review: Off-Peak Membership Proposal

The proposal leaves out the largest financial effect of the change. Once that effect is included, the projected £193,000 gain likely becomes a substantial loss. Several other claims in the author's summary also go beyond what the evidence shows.

## 1. Cannibalisation of existing members (critical)

Section 2 reports that **31% of standard members already visit only in the off-peak window**, and another 22% visit mostly off-peak. Section 6 lets members switch membership type with one month's notice. Yet the revenue projection in Section 5 counts only new members and assumes no existing member downgrades.

- Exclusive off-peak users: 9,600 × 31% ≈ **2,976 members**. Each one who downgrades from £42 to £29 loses £13/month.
- If all of them switch, the loss is about **£38,700/month, or £464,000/year**. That exceeds the entire projected new revenue of £417,600, before class costs.
- Even if only about half switch (~£232,000/year), the £193,200 net becomes roughly **−£39,000**.
- If some of the 2,112 "mostly off-peak" members also switch, the loss could reach about £790,000/year.

These are the members with the strongest reason to downgrade, and the proposal makes switching easy. Section 7 treats the issue only as a perception problem ("may perceive the off-peak price as unfair"). The author's line that "members who want more can upgrade at any time" deals with the wrong direction: the risk is members who want *less* downgrading. Calling this "low-risk" is not supported.

**Needed:** a downgrade scenario analysis, a break-even calculation (how many new members offset each downgrade), and possibly options to limit it, such as a longer notice period, a minimum-term requirement, or launching the tier for new joiners only.

## 2. Revenue projection is overstated even on its own terms

- **Full-year revenue from day one.** £417,600 assumes all 1,200 members pay for all 12 months of year one. In reality recruitment ramps up, so first-year revenue would be much lower.
- **Churn is ignored.** At the 4.8% monthly churn rate for non-class members, or even the hoped-for 2.1%, a meaningful share of recruits leave within the year. Section 4 argues retention matters, but the projection doesn't model it.
- **"Consistent with the survey" can't be checked.** The document never states the catchment population, so readers cannot tell what 19% implies or whether 300 per club is "well within" it.
- **Stated intent overstates conversion.** "Definitely or probably would join" responses typically convert at a small fraction. Combining "probably" with "definitely" inflates the figure further. The survey also seems to show the £29 offer without competing alternatives.

## 3. Weak reasoning on classes and retention

- **Correlation presented as causation.** Members who attend classes churn less, but they are likely more engaged members to begin with. Adding classes will not necessarily move off-peak members "towards 2.1%." The author's claim that classes are "an investment in keeping new members" depends on this unsupported causal link.
- **Contradicted by the proposal's own evidence.** Section 8 reports managers saying **daytime classes are often under-filled**. If existing daytime classes have spare places, adding six more per club per week (£224,400/year, the largest cost line) is hard to justify. New members could fill current classes first.
- **No retention benefit is quantified.** The class cost is fully included in the projection, but the claimed churn reduction does not appear anywhere in the numbers.

## 4. Internal inconsistency on access hours

Section 1 says weekday access ends **before 4 pm**. Section 6 says **until 5 pm**. The difference matters:

- The proposal says the peak runs from 5 pm. A 5 pm cut-off lets off-peak members enter at 4:55 and train well into peak, which is exactly when the floor is at capacity.
- It also changes the number of standard members who qualify as "off-peak users," and so the size of the cannibalisation exposure.

The access window must be fixed before the financials or the access-control changes can be relied on.

## 5. Competitive positioning is not fully addressed

- The budget gyms offer **unrestricted** access at £22–£25, below the proposed **restricted** £29 tier. The target groups, especially students and many retirees, are price-sensitive. The document needs to explain why they would choose a time-limited £29 product over cheaper full access nearby (for example, through quality, classes, or facilities).
- Section 7 says the budget gyms' lower prices mean no price war, but that same price gap is a reason to doubt the recruitment numbers.
- Being "within the £25–£32 market range" shows the price is plausible. It does not show that demand exists.

## 6. Capacity claim needs more support

- "Typical utilisation around 30%" is a weekday daytime average. Retirees and parents of school-age children may cluster at particular times (for example, mid-morning or just after school drop-off), producing local peaks.
- **Weekend utilisation is never reported**, yet off-peak members get all-day weekend access. "No investment in equipment or space" is asserted, not shown.
- Moving existing members into the off-peak tier frees no capacity, because they already train at those times.

## 7. Smaller points

- The Section 7 risk list leaves out cannibalisation, recruitment shortfall, peak-time spillover, and the cost of the access-control changes.
- Implementation costs (access-control reconfiguration, signage, app changes, marketing) are not costed.
- The proposal does not say how success will be measured or what results would trigger a review or withdrawal.

## Summary

| Author's claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| New members cost almost nothing to accommodate | Partly supported for weekdays. Weekend capacity is unknown, and the 5 pm cut-off risks peak overlap. |
| Real demand at £29 | Based on stated intent only. Conversion and catchment size are not established. |
| Classes are an investment in retention | Causal link not shown. Existing daytime classes are under-filled. |
| Conservative projection of 300 per club | Assumes a full year of revenue, zero churn, and no ramp-up. |
| ~£193,000 net revenue | **Ignores downgrades by ~2,976 exclusive off-peak members, which could alone cost up to £464k/year.** |
| Low-risk | Not supported. The main financial risk is not identified. |

**Recommendation:** Do not approve the proposal in its current form. Ask for:
- a revised projection including downgrade scenarios, ramp-up and churn;
- a single, consistent access window;
- evidence that new daytime classes are needed, given that existing ones are under-filled;
- a mitigation plan for cannibalisation.
